title: Transfer of the Critically Ill Patient

references.label: Parmentier-Decrucq 2013
references.citation: Parmentier-Decrucq E, Poissy J, Favory R, et al. Adverse events during intrahospital transport of critically ill patients: incidence and risk factors. Ann Intensive Care. 2013;3(1):10.
references.excerpt: Of 262 transports observed (184 patients), 120 (45.8%) were associated with adverse events. Risk factors were ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure >6 cmH2O, sedation before transport, and fluid loading for intrahospital transports.

references.label: Fanara 2010
references.citation: Fanara B, Manzon C, Barbot O, et al. Recommendations for the intra-hospital transport of critically ill patients. Crit Care. 2010;14(3):R87.
references.excerpt: Basic training, good clinical sense and a risk-benefit analysis are currently the only deciding factors. A critically ill patient, prepared and accompanied by an inexperienced team, is a risky combination.

references.label: Droogh 2012
references.citation: Droogh JM, Kruger HL, Ligtenberg JJ, Zijlstra JG. Simulator-based crew resource management training for interhospital transfer of critically ill patients by a mobile ICU. Jt Comm J Qual Patient Saf. 2012;38(12):554-559.
references.excerpt: The MICU transport program includes simulator-based crew resource management (CRM) training for the intensivists and ICU nurses, who, with the drivers, constitute the MICU crews.

cards.question: How does AAGBI guidance grade inter-hospital transfers?
cards.answer: AAGBI 2009 grades the patient, not the transfer: critical-care dependency Levels 0–3. Level 2 and 3 patients (organ support, advanced respiratory support) must be escorted by competent, trained and experienced personnel — usually a doctor and a nurse or paramedic. The decision to transfer is made consultant-to-consultant; a consultant is not required to travel on every transfer. Staffing, monitoring and vehicle choice escalate with dependency.

cards.question: What is the minimum monitoring required for a critical-care transfer?
cards.answer: ECG, SpO₂, NIBP (every 5 min) or invasive arterial pressure, EtCO₂ if intubated, temperature, and infusion pump status. A means of measuring CVP if cardiovascularly unstable. All monitors must be battery-powered with ≥2× expected transfer duration and a printed transfer chart kept.

cards.question: How do you calculate oxygen requirements for a ventilated transfer?
cards.answer: Oxygen needed (L) = minute ventilation (L/min) × FiO₂ × transfer time (min) × 2 (safety margin) + ventilator driving gas. A full E-cylinder contains ~680 L. Always carry at least double the calculated requirement and a self-inflating bag with reservoir as backup.
